352 − 127: 2 − 7 is not possible, so break a ten: 12 − 7 = 5. Tens: 4 − 2 = 2. Hundreds: 3 − 1 = 2. Answer 225.
If the top tens digit is too small, break 1 hundred into 10 tens.
Check by adding: 225 + 127 = 352.

ex.q: A shop had 430 kites and sold 185. How many kites are left?
st: Ones: 0 − 5 is not possible. Break a ten: 10 − 5 = 5. Now 2 tens are left.
Tens: 2 − 8 is not possible. Break a hundred: 12 − 8 = 4. Now 3 hundreds are left.

topics.rl: Finding how many pages are left to read or how much money is left after shopping uses subtraction.

rv.summary: To subtract, start with the ones. If the top digit is smaller, break 1 ten into 10 ones (or 1 hundred into 10 tens). Check by adding.
focus: Subtract 3-digit numbers with borrowing.
Break a ten or a hundred when needed.
Check by adding the answer and the number taken away.
traps: Don't take the smaller digit from the bigger one. Borrow.
Don't do 8 − 2 when the sum is 2 − 8.
To check, add the answer to the number taken away.

topics.t: Measuring with hand spans and steps
topics.h: How long is your desk? Use your hand span and find out!
p: Length tells how long, how tall or how far something is.
We can measure with body parts: hand spans for a desk, footsteps for a room, arm lengths for a cloth.
A hand span is the stretch from the tip of the thumb to the tip of the little finger.
Different people get different answers, because hand spans are not the same size. A child's span is smaller than a teacher's.
To compare lengths, place things side by side: the longest ponytail, a string as long as the window.

ex.q: Teacher measures the table as 6 spans. Riya measures it as 9 spans. Who has the bigger hand span?
st: The same table needs fewer of a bigger unit.

topics.rl: Tailors used to measure cloth by arm lengths. Now they use a measuring tape so everyone gets the same answer.

rv.summary: Length tells how long, how tall or how far something is. We can measure with hand spans, footsteps and arm lengths, but different people get different answers.
focus: Choose a good body unit for an object.
Compare lengths by placing things side by side.
Explain why counts differ between people.
remember: A hand span: tip of the thumb to tip of the little finger.
A bigger unit fits fewer times: teacher 6 spans, Riya 9 spans.
We need a common unit everyone agrees on.
traps: Length is not weight.
The object does not change when the count changes. The unit changed.
Don't use a tiny unit for a long thing.

topics.h: How far is it from one classroom wall to the other? Steps, a rope, or a stick?
p: To find the distance between two walls, walk heel to toe, or lay a rope or stick again and again, and count.
A good method has no gaps and no overlaps, and uses the same unit every time.
To find the longest and shortest paper strings, place them side by side with one end matching.
To decorate a board, count how many strings fit around its border: top + bottom + 2 sides.

ex.q: A board's border is 4 strings on top, 4 on the bottom and 2 on each side. How many strings in all?

topics.rl: Painters and carpenters measure walls with long tapes before buying paint or wood.

rv.summary: To measure a distance, lay a unit again and again with no gaps and no overlaps. To compare strings, line up one end of each.
focus: Measure without gaps or overlaps.
Compare strings from the same start line.
Count strings around a border.
remember: Use the same unit every time.
A rope twice as long fits half as many times.
traps: Don't leave gaps between steps.
Line up the ends before comparing.
Count all four sides of a border.

topics.h: Cut a thread exactly as long as this line. Not longer, not shorter!
p: To cut a thread as long as a line, lay it along the line from one end to the other and cut where the line ends.
To draw a string longer than a given one, go past its end. Shorter? Stop before the end.
To complete the other half of a moustache, make it the same length as the first half.
To choose the longest string, compare directly: put them side by side with the ends matching.

ex.q: One half of a drawn moustache is 3 boxes long. How long should the other half be?

topics.rl: Tailors match sleeve lengths so both sleeves of a kurta are equal.

rv.summary: To match a length, lay the thread from one end of the line to the other. To draw longer, go past the end; shorter, stop before it.
focus: Cut a thread to match a line.
Draw longer and shorter strings.
Complete equal halves.
remember: Both halves of a moustache are the same length.
traps: Start at the very beginning of the line.
Longer means more boxes, not equal.
Don't add both halves when asked how many to add.

topics.h: Will the big table fit through the door? We cannot lift it to try. Use a string!
p: When two things cannot be placed side by side, use a third thing, like a string or stick.
Measure the table's width with a string and mark it. Then hold the same string against the door.
If the door is wider than the string mark, the table will fit.
Build a block bridge, measure the gap under it, and guess which toys will pass under.
A tall truck or a long ladder held upright may not pass through a school gate.

ex.q: A string matches the width of a cupboard. When held across a door, the string is longer than the door is wide. Will the cupboard pass?
st: The cupboard is as wide as the string.
The door is narrower than the string.

topics.rl: Before buying a sofa or a fridge, families measure the door to check that it will fit through!

rv.summary: When two things cannot be placed side by side, use a third thing like a string to carry the length across and compare.
focus: Compare with a string or stick.
Decide if something will fit through a gap.
Find how much too tall something is.
remember: If the door is wider than the string mark, the table will fit.
A 3-block toy passes under a 5-block gap.
A pole of 7 sticks is 2 too tall for a 5-stick gate.
traps: You don't need to move the table to compare.
Don't reverse the comparison.
A third object is for comparing, not decoration.

topics.h: Is your arm span the same as your height? Let us test it like scientists!
p: Some body measures are often close to each other. We test them to see if they are true for everyone.
Test 1: wrap a string around your head. Is it about 3 of your hand spans?
Test 2: is your forearm (elbow to wrist) about as long as your foot?
Test 3: stretch your arms wide. Is your arm span about the same as your height?
Test many people and record 'yes' or 'no'. If even one person does not fit, it is not true for ALL.

ex.q: 8 friends test arm span = height. 7 say yes and 1 says no. Is it true for all?
ex.a: No, it is true for most but not all

topics.rl: Artists drawing people use body measures like these to get the shape right.

rv.summary: Some body measures are close to each other, like arm span and height. We test many people to see if an idea is true for all.
focus: Test body measure ideas on many people.
Count yes and no answers.
Decide if an idea is true for all.
remember: Head around ≈ 3 hand spans. Forearm (elbow to wrist) ≈ foot.
If even one person does not fit, it is not true for all.
traps: 'Most' does not mean 'all'.
A small test does not prove it for everyone.
The forearm is elbow to wrist, not shoulder to elbow.

topics.h: Hand spans gave everyone a different answer. The metre gives everyone the SAME answer!
p: We need a standard unit so that everyone gets the same measure.
The metre (m) is a standard unit of length. A metre rod or a measuring tape shows 1 metre.
Make a one-metre rope: lay a rope along a metre rod and cut it at the end.
Mark 1 metre from the floor on a wall. Stand against it to see if you are taller or shorter than 1 metre.
A door is about 2 metres tall. A classroom may be about 6 to 8 metres long.

ex.q: A rope is laid along a metre rod 3 times to measure a mat. How long is the mat?

topics.rl: Cloth shops sell cloth by the metre, and sports tracks are measured in metres.

rv.summary: The metre (m) is a standard unit of length. Everyone who uses a metre gets the same measure.
focus: Explain why we need a standard unit.
Make a 1-metre rope.
Add and take away lengths in metres.
remember: A metre rod or tape shows 1 metre.
A door is about 2 m tall. A big stride is about 1 m.
3 lays of a metre rope = 3 m.
traps: Body units are not the same for all. Metres are.
Above the 1 m mark means taller, not shorter.
The same tape gives the same answer for everyone.

topics.h: Is your friend taller than a metre rod? Is a door? Is a pencil? Let us sort!
p: Stand friends next to a 1-metre mark. Sort them: taller than 1 m, or shorter than 1 m.
Many Class 3 children are a little taller than 1 metre.
Objects can be longer than, shorter than or about equal to 1 metre.
Longer than 1 m: a door, a bed, a classroom. Shorter: a pencil, a book, a shoe. About 1 m: a metre rod, a big stride.

ex.q: Sort: bed, eraser, metre rod.
st: A bed is long: longer than 1 m.
A metre rod is exactly 1 m.
ex.a: Longer: bed; shorter: eraser; equal: metre rod

topics.rl: At amusement parks, some rides have a height mark. You must be taller than it to ride!

rv.summary: Objects and people can be longer than, shorter than or about 1 metre. A 1-metre mark on a wall helps us sort.
focus: Sort objects as longer, shorter or about 1 m.
Sort friends against a 1-metre mark.
Add and compare the counts.
remember: Longer than 1 m: door, bed, classroom.
Shorter than 1 m: pencil, book, shoe.
About 1 m: metre rod, big stride.
traps: Below the mark means shorter.
2 m is more than 1 m.
Check every item in a list.

topics.h: Fold a 1-metre rope in half. Now you have a half-metre! Fold again for a quarter-metre!
p: Fold a 1-metre rope in half and cut: each piece is half a metre.
Fold the half-metre in half again: each piece is a quarter metre.
2 half metres make 1 metre. 4 quarter metres make 1 metre. 2 quarter metres make a half metre.
Sort objects: less than a quarter metre (an eraser), about half a metre (a school bag), about 1 metre.
Measure a long jump with a metre rope: 1 metre and a half metre is one and a half metres.

ex.q: Leela jumps 1 metre rope + 1 half-metre rope + 1 quarter-metre rope. How far?
st: 1 m + half m = one and a half m

topics.rl: Cloth shops sell half a metre or a quarter metre of ribbon too.

rv.summary: Fold a 1-metre rope in half to get half metres, and in half again to get quarter metres.
focus: Make half and quarter metres.
Know how many halves and quarters make a metre.
Measure with metres and parts of metres.
remember: 2 half metres = 1 metre. 4 quarter metres = 1 metre.
3 m and a half m = 3 and a half metres.
traps: Folding once gives halves, not quarters.
A half-metre rope is not a full metre.
4 quarter metres is 1 metre, not 4 metres.

topics.h: Close your eyes and cut a thread you think is 1 metre long. Now check with a metre rod. How close were you?
p: Estimate 1 metre by cutting a thread, then check it with a metre rod.
To cut a rope into 4 equal pieces, you need only 3 cuts.
In general, the number of cuts is one less than the number of pieces.
Count how many of your footsteps make 1 metre. It may be 4 or 5 for a child.
Measure a classroom wall with a metre rope: lay it end to end and count.

ex.q: How many cuts are needed to cut a ribbon into 6 equal pieces?

topics.rl: A carpenter cutting a plank into pieces must plan the number of cuts, not just the pieces.

rv.summary: Estimate 1 metre and check with a metre rod. To cut something into equal pieces, the cuts are one less than the pieces.
focus: Estimate and check 1 metre.
Find the number of cuts for some pieces.
Count footsteps for a metre.
remember: A child may take 4 or 5 footsteps for 1 metre.
traps: Cuts are not equal to pieces.
10 pieces need 9 cuts, not 10.
The metre does not change. Step sizes do.

topics.h: 2, 4, 6, 8... who do we appreciate? Number patterns, of course!
p: A pattern follows a rule again and again.
Some patterns grow by adding: 2, 4, 6, 8 (add 2 each time).
Some patterns get smaller by taking away: 50, 45, 40 (take away 5 each time).
Find the rule by looking at how each number changes to the next.
Even numbers end in 0, 2, 4, 6 or 8. Odd numbers end in 1, 3, 5, 7 or 9. They take turns: even, odd, even, odd.

ex.q: What comes next: 3, 7, 11, 15, ___?

topics.rl: House numbers on one side of a street often go 2, 4, 6, 8 and on the other side 1, 3, 5, 7.

rv.summary: A number pattern follows a rule again and again, like add 2 or take away 5. Find the rule by seeing how each number changes.
focus: Find the rule of a pattern.
Find the next or missing number.
Tell even and odd numbers.
remember: Even numbers end in 0, 2, 4, 6, 8. Odd end in 1, 3, 5, 7, 9.
traps: Check if the pattern goes up or down.
Don't add 1 when the jump is bigger.
Doubling is not adding 2.

topics.h: Party flags, bangles and rangoli all have patterns. Can you guess what comes next?
p: A repeating pattern has a part that comes again and again: 🔴🔵🔴🔵.
The part that repeats is called the core. In red, blue, blue, red, blue, blue, the core is red, blue, blue.
A growing pattern gets bigger at each step: 1 dot, 2 dots, 3 dots.
To find what comes next, find the core or the rule first.

ex.q: Party flags go: green, yellow, yellow, green, yellow, yellow, ___. What comes next?
st: The core is green, yellow, yellow.
After the second yellow, the core starts again.

topics.rl: Borders of saris, bead necklaces and paper chains for parties all show patterns.

rv.summary: A repeating pattern has a core that comes again and again. A growing pattern gets bigger at each step.
focus: Find the core of a repeating pattern.
Find what comes next.
Tell repeating and growing patterns apart.
remember: Core of red, blue, blue, red, blue, blue is red, blue, blue.
traps: Don't just repeat the last item. Follow the core.
Count every item in the core.
A repeating pattern is not a growing pattern.

topics.h: Fold a paper butterfly down the middle. Both wings match perfectly. That's symmetry!
p: A shape is symmetrical if one half is a mirror image of the other half.
The fold line that makes two matching halves is called the line of symmetry.
Letters like A, H, M, O, T, U, V, W, X and Y have matching halves when folded along a standing line down the middle.
Some shapes have more than one line of symmetry. A square has 4. A circle has many.
Rangoli and kolam designs are often symmetrical.

ex.q: How many lines of symmetry does a long rectangle, like a door, have?
st: Fold it along a standing line down the middle: the halves match.
Fold it along a sleeping line across the middle: the halves match.
Fold it corner to corner: the halves do NOT match.

topics.rl: Butterflies, leaves, diyas, the Taj Mahal and many rangoli designs are symmetrical.

rv.summary: A shape is symmetrical if one half is a mirror image of the other. The fold line is the line of symmetry.
focus: Find symmetrical letters and shapes.
Count lines of symmetry.
Complete a symmetrical design.
remember: A, H, M, O, T, U, V, W, X, Y match when folded down the middle.
A square has 4 lines of symmetry. A circle has many.
A long rectangle has 2 lines of symmetry.
traps: A rectangle does not have 4 lines like a square.
The line of symmetry is not the edge.
Read NOT in the question.

topics.h: Chintu fills a bucket with a big glass. Mintu uses a small glass. Who needs more glasses?
p: A bigger glass holds more, so FEWER big glasses fill a bucket.
A smaller glass holds less, so MORE small glasses are needed.
To compare two containers, fill each and pour into same-sized glasses. The one that fills more glasses holds more.
Use words: holds more, holds less, holds the most, holds the least.

ex.q: A jug fills 6 glasses. A bottle fills 4 of the same glasses. Which holds more?

topics.rl: At a wedding, big pots of water are poured into small glasses to serve guests.

rv.summary: A bigger glass holds more, so fewer big glasses fill a bucket. To compare containers fairly, pour each into same-sized glasses.
focus: Compare containers by counting same-sized glasses.
Use holds more, less, most and least.
Know that bigger units need fewer fills.
remember: Bigger glass → fewer fills. Smaller glass → more fills.
Jug 6 glasses, bottle 4 glasses: the jug holds more.
traps: More fills does not mean the glass is bigger.
Don't use glasses of different sizes to compare.
Height alone does not tell which holds more.

topics.h: A bucket or a cup: which one would you use to fill a bathtub? Let's compare how much things hold!
p: Capacity is how much a container can hold.
We can compare by filling one container and pouring it into another.
We can measure with small cups or glasses: a jug may hold 6 glasses of water.
Litre (L) is the standard unit for liquids like milk, water and oil.
Small amounts are measured in millilitres (mL). 1 litre = 1000 millilitres.

ex.q: A bucket holds 10 mugs of water. A pot holds 4 mugs. How many more mugs does the bucket hold?

topics.rl: Milk comes in 1 litre and half-litre packets, and water bottles are often 1 litre.

rv.summary: Capacity is how much a container can hold. We compare by pouring, measure with cups, and use litres (L) and millilitres (mL).
focus: Compare containers by pouring.
Use litres for liquids.
Know litres and millilitres.
traps: 1 litre is 1000 mL, not 100 mL.
Kilogram is for weight, not liquids.
The container that overflows holds less.

topics.h: How many ladles of dal fill one glass? Guess first, then pour!
p: Guess how many small containers fill a big one, then check by pouring.
The smaller the measuring vessel, the more times you must fill it.
If 1 jug fills 4 glasses, 3 jugs fill 4 + 4 + 4 = 12 glasses.
If 1 glass takes 5 ladles, 4 glasses take 20 ladles.
Choose a suitable vessel: a ladle to serve dal, a jug to pour water, a bucket to water plants.

ex.q: 1 glass takes 3 ladles. How many ladles for 4 glasses?

topics.rl: In a langar or a school mid-day meal, food is served with ladles of the same size so everyone gets the same.

rv.summary: Guess how many small containers fill a big one, then check by pouring. The smaller the vessel, the more times you fill it.
focus: Find fills using equal groups.
Choose a suitable vessel for a job.
Compare only with the same unit.
remember: Ladle for dal, jug for water, bucket for plants.
traps: Don't add when you should multiply.
Small vessels need more fills, not fewer.
3 glasses and 3 cups may not be the same amount.

topics.h: Why does the milkman use a measuring can, not just any glass?
p: Glasses are of different sizes, so a milkman uses a standard measure to give everyone the same amount.
A litre (L) is a standard unit to measure liquids like milk, water and oil.
Some containers hold more than 1 litre (a bucket), some less (a glass), some exactly 1 litre (a 1-litre bottle).
Estimate first: a bucket may hold about 10 litres. Then check with a 1-litre bottle.
Save water: reuse bottles and close taps. Every litre counts!

ex.q: A bucket is filled using a 1-litre bottle 12 times. How much does it hold?

topics.rl: Milk packets, oil bottles and water cans are sold in litres.

rv.summary: A litre (L) is a standard unit for liquids, so everyone gets the same amount. Some containers hold more than 1 litre and some less.
focus: Explain why we need a standard measure.
Sort containers as more or less than 1 litre.
Estimate and check in litres.
remember: A bucket holds more than 1 L. A glass holds less.
Save water: close taps, reuse bottles.
traps: Any glass is not a fair measure.
Litres are for liquids, not weight or length.
Don't pick a wasteful habit as saving water.

topics.h: A 1-litre bottle poured into 2 equal bottles gives 2 half-litres!
p: Half a litre is one of 2 equal parts of a litre.
A quarter litre is one of 4 equal parts of a litre.
2 half-litres make 1 litre.
4 quarter-litres make 1 litre.
2 quarter-litres make a half litre.

ex.q: How many quarter-litre cups fill a 1-litre jug?

topics.rl: Milk packets often come in half-litre size. Small juice packs are about a quarter litre or less.

rv.summary: Half a litre is one of 2 equal parts of a litre. A quarter litre is one of 4 equal parts.
focus: Know how many halves and quarters make a litre.
Add half and quarter litres.
Compare half and quarter litres.
remember: 3 half-litre packets = 1 and a half litres.
traps: A quarter litre is less than a half, even though 4 is bigger than 2.
Don't count each half-litre packet as 1 litre.
2 quarter-litre glasses are half a litre, not 2 litres.

topics.h: Hold a book in one hand and a pencil in the other. Which hand feels pulled down?
p: Hold one object in each hand. The heavier one pulls your hand down more.
Record your results: write which object in each pair is heavier.
On a pan balance, we can weigh things using coins, erasers or matchboxes filled with sand as units.
A pencil box that balances 12 coins is heavier than a sharpener that balances 3 coins.
Arrange objects from lightest to heaviest. Move books between bags to make two bags about the same weight.

ex.q: Bag A has 5 books and bag B has 3 books (all the same). How can you make them equal?
st: Move 1 book from A to B.
ex.a: Move 1 book from A to B

topics.rl: Vegetable sellers use a pan balance with weights to sell sabzi.

rv.summary: Hold one object in each hand: the heavier one pulls down more. On a pan balance we can weigh with coins, erasers or sand matchboxes as units.
focus: Compare weights by holding.
Weigh with non-standard units on a balance.
Order objects from lightest to heaviest.
remember: Pencil box 12 coins, sharpener 3 coins: 9 coins heavier.
Use units that are all the same.
Bags of 5 and 3 books: move 1 to make 4 and 4.
traps: Bigger does not always mean heavier.
Don't use units of different sizes.
Read whether the order is lightest first or heaviest first.

topics.h: Is a big balloon heavier than a small stone? Let's put them on a balance and see!
p: Weight tells us how heavy something is.
On a balance, the heavier side goes down and the lighter side goes up.
Big things are not always heavier! A balloon is big but very light.
Kilogram (kg) is used to weigh things like rice, vegetables and people.
Light things are weighed in grams (g). 1 kilogram = 1000 grams.

ex.q: On a balance, a bag of potatoes goes down and a packet of chips goes up. Which is heavier?

topics.rl: The sabziwala weighs vegetables in kilograms, and the jeweller weighs gold in grams.

rv.summary: Weight tells how heavy something is. On a balance, the heavier side goes down. We use kilograms (kg) and grams (g).
focus: Read a balance.
Use kilograms and grams.
Add and take away weights.
remember: Heavier side goes down, lighter side goes up.
A balloon is big but very light.
traps: Bigger things are not always heavier.
Litre is for liquids, not weight.
1 kg is 1000 g, not 100 g.

topics.h: A 1 kg packet of salt. Is your school bag heavier or lighter than that?
p: Things at home that weigh 1 kg: a 1 kg packet of sugar, atta or salt.
Guess if something is lighter or heavier than 1 kg, then check on a balance with a 1 kg weight.
Half a kilogram is half of 1 kg. 2 half-kilograms make 1 kg.
A quarter kilogram is a quarter of 1 kg. 4 quarter-kilograms make 1 kg; 2 quarter-kilograms make half a kg.
About half a kg: a small papaya. About a quarter kg: a big apple or a large onion.

ex.q: A shopkeeper puts two half-kilogram weights on one pan. What weight is that?

topics.rl: Vegetable shops use 1 kg, half kg and quarter kg weights every day.

rv.summary: A 1 kg packet of sugar or atta weighs 1 kg. Half a kilogram and a quarter kilogram are parts of 1 kg.
focus: Sort things as lighter or heavier than 1 kg.
Know half and quarter kilograms.
Make 1 kg from smaller weights.
remember: Small papaya ≈ half kg. Big apple ≈ quarter kg.
traps: Don't count each half-kg as 1 kg.
4 quarter-kg weights make 1 kg, not 2.
A big watermelon is heavier than 1 kg.

topics.h: The milkman, the grocer and the water tanker all need maths. Let's solve their puzzles!
p: We add litres to litres and kilograms to kilograms.
Always write the unit with the answer, like 5 L or 8 kg.
Read the story: 'in all' means add and 'left' means take away.
To find how many small jugs fill a big bucket, count equal groups.

ex.q: A milkman has 20 litres of milk. He sells 12 litres. How much milk is left?

topics.rl: At home, we buy oil in litres and flour in kilograms, and we use maths to know how much is left.

rv.summary: We add litres to litres and kilograms to kilograms, and always write the unit. 'In all' means add and 'left' means take away.
focus: Solve story sums with litres and kilograms.
Choose add or take away from the words.
Choose litres or kilograms for a thing.
remember: Liquids in litres. Solid things in kilograms.
traps: Don't forget the unit in the answer.
Don't add when the story says 'left'.
Don't mix up weight and capacity.

topics.h: Three balls look the same, but one is heavier. You may use the balance only ONCE. Can you find it?
p: Put one ball on each pan and keep the third aside.
If one pan goes down, that ball is the heavy one.
If the pans balance, the ball kept aside is the heavy one.
To order 3 balls from heaviest to lightest, compare two at a time and keep track of the results.
If A is heavier than B, and B is heavier than C, then A is heavier than C.

ex.q: Balls P, Q, R. P goes down against Q. Q goes down against R. Order them heaviest first.

topics.rl: Detectives and scientists use clever tests like this to find the odd one with few tries.

rv.summary: To find the heavy ball among 3, put one on each pan and keep one aside. If the pans balance, the one aside is heavy.
focus: Find the heavy ball in one weighing.
Order balls from heaviest to lightest.
Read up, down and balanced pans.
remember: Pan goes down = heavier. Pan goes up = lighter.
If A > B and B > C, then A > C.
traps: You don't need to try every pair.
Up means lighter, not heavier.
Don't mix up the order heaviest and lightest.

topics.h: Kishan has 364 rose plants and gets 52 more. How many plants now? Draw a box diagram!
p: A box diagram: a long box for the whole, small boxes for the parts.
If both parts are known, add them: 364 + 52.
Add ones: 4 + 2 = 6. Tens: 6 + 5 = 11 tens = 1 hundred 1 ten. Hundreds: 3 + 1 = 4. Answer 416.
Make your own story from a box diagram: whole ?, parts 245 and 38 → 'Kishan sold 245 marigolds and 38 roses...'
topics.rl: Nurseries count plants every day: new plants come in and some are sold.

rv.summary: A box diagram shows the whole and its parts. If both parts are known, add them. If the whole and one part are known, subtract.
focus: Add 3-digit and 2-digit numbers with carrying.
Use a box diagram to choose add or subtract.
Make a story from a box diagram.
traps: Don't forget to carry the hundred.
Two parts joined is an adding story, not a take-away story.

topics.h: 230 − 75. There are no ones to take 5 from! Break a ten!
p: Dienes blocks: flats are hundreds, rods are tens, small cubes are ones.
If there are not enough ones, break 1 ten rod into 10 ones.
If there are not enough tens, break 1 hundred flat into 10 tens.
230 − 75: break a ten → 2 hundreds, 2 tens, 10 ones. 10 − 5 = 5. Tens 2 − 7? Break a hundred → 12 tens − 7 = 5. Hundreds 1. Answer 155.

ex.q: Subtract 230 − 75 with blocks.

topics.rl: When you pay ₹100 for a ₹35 item, the shopkeeper breaks the ₹100 into smaller notes for change. That is regrouping!

rv.summary: Dienes blocks show hundreds (flats), tens (rods) and ones (cubes). When there are not enough ones or tens, break a bigger block.
focus: Subtract using Dienes blocks.
Break a ten into 10 ones or a hundred into 10 tens.
Check by adding back.
traps: Don't take the smaller digit from the bigger one. Break a block.
After breaking a ten, take 1 away from the tens.
To check, add the answer and the part taken away.

topics.h: On a grid from 451 to 530, step down to add 10. Step right to add 1. What adds 100?
